subtype: Approach: analysis paralysis over comparing many paths [Pitfall]
passage:
"Vidya, what is this?" asked her brother Hemant, holding up a printout from the sofa arm. It was a table with seven columns.

"My comparison. Data science, managing products, user-experience design, cloud. Salary, learning curve, demand, work-life balance..."

"How long have you been doing this?"

"Since April. I keep adding columns."

"It's September."

She folded her arms. "I want to choose properly. I can't just jump."

"Have you tried any of them? Even a free hour of a course?"

"No. I need more information first."

"More tables won't give it to you. Pick the top two and try each for two weeks."

Vidya stared at the table. "Five months," she said. "I've done five months of columns."

qa.q: How many columns did Vidya's table have?
What is Vidya feeling when she says she cannot just jump?
qa.a: Vidya feels anxious about choosing wrongly, wanting certainty before committing, which is why she keeps adding columns.

qa.q: What could Vidya do next instead of adding another column, and why?
qa.a: Vidya could pick two paths and try a short course or task for each, because trying provides information that comparing on paper cannot.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Vidya's table?
qa.a: Hemant sees months of effort that have not moved her forward, and is trying to help her without hurting her feelings.

grounding: The person compares data science, product management, UX and cloud for months, making tables but never trying one.

subtype: Approach: analysis paralysis over comparing many paths [Pitfall]
passage:
For seven months I compared paths. UX, cloud, data science, product management. I made a spreadsheet with twelve columns: salary, course cost, demand, how much coding, how much talking to people. I read every article. I watched every "day in the life" video.
Every week I added rows. Every week the answer changed.
My friend Pankaj finally asked, "Have you tried any of them? Even for a weekend?"
I hadn't. Not one tutorial, not one project. I was scared that trying one meant closing the others, so I kept comparing.
Meanwhile, two people from my batch who'd simply started a UX course had portfolios. I had a very beautiful spreadsheet.
I'm Jaya, and I've learned that comparing only helps when you have something real to compare. Next weekend I'm trying one UX exercise and one data exercise. Then the spreadsheet can have actual data.

qa.q: How many columns did Jaya's spreadsheet have?
Why did Jaya keep comparing instead of trying?
qa.a: Jaya felt scared that trying one path meant closing the others, so comparing felt safer.

qa.q: What would you change first in Jaya's approach, and why?
qa.a: I would try one small exercise from each path early on, because real experience adds information that more research cannot.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel after asking that question?
qa.a: Pankaj may feel a little worried for a friend but relieved that the question finally pushed Jaya toward trying something.

grounding: Shows a person comparing several career paths for months in tables without trying any, falling behind peers who simply started.

subtype: Approach: analysis paralysis over comparing many paths [Pitfall]
passage:
Career services note, month 4. Written by Vandana, career counsellor.
Ishita came in today for the fourth time this term. She brought a new version of her comparison table: UX design, data science, cloud engineering, product management, now with fifteen criteria and scores for each. The scores had changed since last month, though nothing in her life had.
I asked what she had tried. She looked at the table for a while, then said, "Nothing yet. I keep thinking one more article will settle it."
She seemed tired and a little embarrassed. I noticed she has missed two application deadlines for internships in all four areas while researching.
What I did next: I suggested she stop adding criteria and instead pick two paths to test for two weeks each, with one small task for each. She chose UX and data. We agreed she would bring the finished tasks, not a new table, to our next meeting in three weeks.

qa.q: How many criteria did Ishita's new table have?
How did Ishita seem to feel when asked what she had tried?
qa.a: She seemed tired and a little embarrassed, admitting she had tried nothing and hoped another article would settle it.

qa.q: What else could Ishita do if both tests go well?
qa.a: She could do a slightly longer project in each or talk to people working in both, so the next choice rests on more real experience.

qa.q: How does Ishita's situation look to the counsellor?
qa.a: The counsellor sees a capable student stuck in comparison and missing deadlines, and steers her toward small real tests.

grounding: Shows a person comparing four career paths for months with ever-changing tables but never trying one, and missing chances as a result.
